course.title: React - Build Modern Web Apps
course.description: Master React hooks, routing, state management and deploy production-ready apps.

lessons.title: Components & JSX
lessons.body:
Components & JSX

A React app is built from components — small, reusable functions that return what should appear on screen. A component is just a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter: function Greet() { return <h1>Hello</h1>; }. Components can be reused anywhere: use <Greet /> ten times and you get ten greetings.

JSX is the HTML-like syntax inside components. It looks like HTML but it is JavaScript: put any expression inside curly braces — <h1>Hello {name}</h1> shows the value of name. Two JSX rules trip up beginners: use className instead of class (because class is a reserved word in JavaScript), and every component must return a single root element, so wrap siblings in one <div> or a fragment <>...</>. Components receive data through props — <Greet name="Sid" /> makes props.name equal to "Sid" inside Greet.

function Greet({ name }) {
  return <h1 className="title">Hello {name}</h1>;
}
// <Greet name="Sid" /> renders: Hello Sid

Step by step: the component receives name as a prop, destructures it in the function signature, and the JSX expression {name} prints its value into the heading.

  • Key points
  • A component is a function returning JSX; its name must start with a capital letter.
  • JavaScript expressions go inside curly braces in JSX.
  • Use className, not class, and return a single root element.

mcqs.q: What is JSX?
options: An HTML-like syntax for writing UI inside JavaScript
mcqs.why: JSX lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript; React compiles it into JavaScript calls that build the UI.

mcqs.q: What is a React component?
options: A reusable function that returns JSX describing part of the UI
mcqs.why: Components are functions (or classes) that return JSX; apps are built by composing them.

mcqs.q: How do you show the value of a JavaScript variable inside JSX?
options: By writing it as plain text
mcqs.why: Curly braces in JSX mark a JavaScript expression, so {name} evaluates the variable and prints its value.

mcqs.q: Why do you write className instead of class in JSX?
options: It makes the page load faster
Because class is a reserved word in JavaScript
Because React does not support CSS classes
It is only a style preference
mcqs.why: class is reserved in JavaScript, so JSX uses className for the HTML class attribute.

mcqs.q: What happens if a component returns two sibling elements with no wrapper?
options: JSX throws an error: a component must return a single root element
The page goes blank with no error
mcqs.why: A component must return one root element; wrap siblings in a div or a fragment <>...</>.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.answer: The template literal ${name} is replaced by the value of name, so it prints Hello Sid.

lessons.title: Hooks: useState & useEffect
lessons.body:
Hooks: useState & useEffect

Hooks let function components hold state and react to changes. useState is the most common: const [count, setCount] = useState(0) creates a state value count starting at 0 and a setter setCount. Calling setCount(5) updates the value and tells React to re-render the component with the new value. Never assign to count directly — only the setter triggers a re-render.

useEffect handles side effects — things outside rendering, like fetching data or setting a timer. It runs after the component renders. The dependency array controls when it re-runs: useEffect(fn, []) with an empty array runs once after the first render, while useEffect(fn, [count]) re-runs whenever count changes. Leave the array out entirely and the effect runs after every render. Two rules apply to all hooks: call them only at the top level of a component (never inside loops, conditions or nested functions) and only from React components or other hooks.

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    document.title = `Count: ${count}`;
  }, [count]);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}

Step by step: clicking the button calls setCount(count + 1), React re-renders with the new count, and the effect updates the page title because count is in its dependency array.

  • Key points
  • useState returns [value, setter]; only the setter triggers a re-render.
  • useEffect runs after render; the dependency array controls when it re-runs.
  • Hooks go at the top level of a component — never in loops or conditions.

mcqs.q: What does const [count, setCount] = useState(0) give you?
options: A variable count and a function setCount that updates it and re-renders
A reference to the DOM element
mcqs.why: useState returns a pair: the current state value and a setter function that updates it and triggers a re-render.

mcqs.q: What happens when you call setCount(5)?
options: count is set to 5 but nothing re-renders
The state updates to 5 and React re-renders the component
mcqs.why: The setter updates the state and schedules a re-render so the UI shows the new value.

mcqs.q: What is useEffect used for?
options: Side effects such as fetching data or setting timers, run after render
mcqs.why: useEffect runs code after rendering for work outside the render itself, like data fetching and subscriptions.

mcqs.q: What does an empty dependency array [] in useEffect mean?
options: The effect runs once, after the first render
The effect runs after every render
The effect runs only when the component unmounts
mcqs.why: With no dependencies to watch, the effect has nothing that can trigger a re-run, so it runs once on mount.

mcqs.q: Which of these breaks the Rules of Hooks?
options: Calling useState at the top of a component
Calling useState inside an if block
Calling useState in a custom hook
Calling two useState hooks in one component
mcqs.why: Hooks must be called in the same order on every render, so they cannot be inside conditions, loops or nested functions.

tasks.title: Trace the variables
tasks.prompt: A Counter starts at 0. The button is clicked twice. What number does the button show after the second click?
tasks.answer: Each click adds 1: after click 1 the count is 1, after click 2 it is 2, and the button renders the current count.
tasks.hint: Trace count through each click: what is count when the second click runs?

lessons.title: React Router
lessons.body:
React Router

A single-page app has no real page loads, so React Router provides client-side routing: the URL changes and a different component renders, without the browser fetching a new page. Wrap the app in <BrowserRouter>, list the routes inside <Routes>, and map each path to a component with <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />.

Navigate with <Link to="/about">About</Link> instead of a plain <a href> — a Link updates the URL and renders the new route without a full page reload, so state is preserved. Dynamic parts of a URL are parameters: a route /users/:id matches /users/42, and useParams() inside the component returns { id: "42" }. A catch-all route path="*" renders a "page not found" component for unknown URLs.

import { BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, Link } from "react-router-dom";
<BrowserRouter>
  <Link to="/about">About</Link>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

Step by step: clicking the Link changes the URL to /about, the Routes list finds the matching Route, and the About component renders — no page reload, no lost state.

  • Key points
  • <BrowserRouter> wraps the app; <Routes> holds the <Route> list.
  • <Link> navigates without a full page reload; a plain <a> reloads the page.
  • URL parameters like :id are read with useParams().

mcqs.q: Which component must wrap the app for React Router to work?
mcqs.why: BrowserRouter provides the routing context (history and location) that Routes, Link and the hooks need.

mcqs.q: What does <Route path="/about" element={<About />} /> do?
options: It renders About only when the URL is /about
It fetches the About page from the server
mcqs.why: A Route renders its element only when the current URL matches its path.

mcqs.q: Why use <Link> instead of a plain <a href> in a React app?
options: Link navigates without a full page reload, so app state is preserved
Plain anchors are banned in React
mcqs.why: Link updates the URL through the router and renders the new route client-side; a plain anchor reloads the whole page.

mcqs.q: For the route /users/:id, what does useParams() return when the URL is /users/42?
mcqs.why: useParams returns an object of the matched parameters, with values as strings: { id: "42" }.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of a Route with path="*"?
options: It matches only the home page
It is a catch-all that renders for any unmatched URL, such as a 404 page
It loads all routes at once
mcqs.why: The * path matches anything, so it is used as the last route to render a Not Found page.

tasks.title: Fill in the blank
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing component so clicking About navigates without a full page reload.
tasks.answer: Link is React Router's navigation component: it updates the URL and renders the matching route client-side.
tasks.hint: Which component navigates without reloading the page?

lessons.title: State Management Basics
lessons.body:
State Management Basics

State is data that changes over time, and in React it flows one way: down. A parent passes data to a child through props, and the child cannot change the parent's state directly — it calls a function the parent passed down instead. When two sibling components need the same data, lift the state up: move it into their nearest common parent and pass it down to both.

Passing props through many layers just to reach a deep child is called prop drilling, and it makes components hard to change. The Context API fixes it: create a context, wrap the tree in a Provider with the value, and any deep component reads it with useContext — no middlemen. For state with many related values and transitions, useReducer groups the logic into one reducer function instead of many separate useState calls. The rule of thumb: local state with useState first, lift state up when siblings share it, Context when many components need it, and a reducer when updates get complicated.

// Lifting state up: the parent owns the shared value
function Parent() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState("light");
  return <><Header theme={theme} /><Footer setTheme={setTheme} /></>;
}

Step by step: the theme lives in the parent, Header receives it as a prop to display, and Footer receives the setter so it can change the theme for both.

  • Key points
  • Data flows down through props; children change parent state via functions passed down.
  • Lift shared state into the nearest common parent of the components that need it.
  • Context avoids prop drilling; useReducer organises complex state updates.

mcqs.q: When two sibling components need the same data, what should you do?
options: Duplicate the state in both components
Lift the state up into their nearest common parent
Store it in a global variable
Fetch it twice from the server
mcqs.why: Lifting state up keeps one source of truth in the shared parent, which passes it down to both siblings.

mcqs.q: In React, which direction does data flow?
options: One way: down from parent to child through props
Only upward, from child to parent
mcqs.why: React data flows down via props; children communicate upward only by calling functions the parent passed down.

mcqs.q: What problem does the Context API solve?
options: Prop drilling: passing props through many layers to reach a deep child
mcqs.why: Context lets any deep component read a shared value directly, without every layer in between passing it along.

mcqs.q: When is useReducer a better choice than several useState calls?
options: When the state is a single boolean
When the state has many related values and transitions
When the component has no state
When you need to fetch data
mcqs.why: useReducer groups related state and its update logic into one reducer function, which stays readable as complexity grows.

mcqs.q: What is prop drilling?
options: Passing data through many layers of components just to reach a deep child
Drilling a hole in the component tree
A way to fetch props from the server
mcqs.why: Prop drilling is threading props through intermediate components that do not use the data themselves.

tasks.title: Fill in the blank
tasks.prompt: Complete the sentence about passing data through many layers.
tasks.code: Passing data through many layers of components just to reach a deep child is called prop ___.
tasks.answer: Prop drilling is threading props through components that do not need the data themselves; Context is the usual fix.
tasks.hint: Which word describes threading props down through layers?

lessons.title: Deploy a React App
lessons.body:
Deploy a React App

Deploying turns your development project into a live website. First build it: npm run build runs the production build, which bundles, minifies and optimises your code into static files. With Create React App the output goes into a build/ folder; with Vite it goes into dist/. Those files are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no Node server is needed to serve them.

Upload that folder to a static host such as Netlify, Vercel or GitHub Pages and the app is live. One catch: client-side routing. When a user refreshes on /about, the host must serve index.html for that URL instead of a 404, because the route only exists inside your JavaScript — this is called the SPA fallback, and Netlify and Vercel handle it with a one-line redirect rule. Environment variables keep secrets out of the code: in Create React App, variables starting with REACT_APP_ are embedded at build time, so never put a real secret in one — anything in the bundle is visible to users.

npm run build        # creates the production bundle
# Create React App -> build/ folder
# Vite             -> dist/ folder
# Then upload that folder to Netlify, Vercel or GitHub Pages

Step by step: build the bundle, upload the output folder to a static host, and add the SPA fallback so refreshing on any route serves index.html.

  • Key points
  • npm run build creates the optimised production bundle.
  • A React build is static files — any static host can serve it.
  • Hosts need an SPA fallback so client-side routes do not 404 on refresh.

mcqs.q: Which command creates the production-ready bundle of a React app?
mcqs.why: npm run build bundles, minifies and optimises the app into static files ready for hosting.

mcqs.q: Where does Create React App put the production build output?
mcqs.why: The build script writes the optimised static files into build/ (Vite uses dist/ instead).

mcqs.q: Which of these can host a React production build?
options: Any static host such as Netlify, Vercel or GitHub Pages
mcqs.why: The build output is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so any static file host can serve it.

mcqs.q: What is the SPA fallback a host needs for a React Router app?
options: Serving index.html for any route so client-side routing works on refresh
mcqs.why: Routes like /about exist only in JavaScript, so the host must return index.html for them instead of a 404.

mcqs.q: In Create React App, which variables are embedded into the build?
options: None — environment variables never reach the browser
mcqs.why: CRA embeds variables prefixed with REACT_APP_ at build time; anything in the bundle is visible, so secrets must never go there.

tasks.title: Fill in the blank
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing word to create the production bundle.
tasks.code: npm run ___  # creates the production-ready bundle
tasks.answer: npm run build runs the build script, which bundles and minifies the app into static files.
tasks.hint: Which npm script builds the app for production?

lessons.title: Performance Optimisation in React
lessons.body:
Performance Optimisation in React

React is fast by default, but re-renders add up. A component re-renders when its state, props or parent change — and a big list re-rendering on every keystroke feels sluggish. React.memo wraps a component so React skips re-rendering it when its props have not changed: const UserRow = React.memo(function UserRow({ user }) { ... }).

For expensive calculations, useMemo caches a value and only recomputes it when its dependencies change: const sorted = useMemo(() => items.sort(), [items]). useCallback does the same for functions, so a memoised child does not re-render just because its parent passed a brand-new function each time. For big apps, split the code: React.lazy(() => import("./Admin")) loads a heavy page only when the user opens it, wrapped in <Suspense> with a loading fallback. And always give list items a stable key — keys tell React which item is which, so it updates only the rows that changed instead of rebuilding the whole list.

const sorted = useMemo(() => items.sort((a, b) => a - b), [items]);
const onSave = useCallback(() => save(items), [items]);
const Admin = React.lazy(() => import("./Admin"));

Step by step: useMemo re-sorts only when items changes, useCallback keeps the same save function until items changes, and React.lazy defers loading Admin until it is needed.

  • Key points
  • React.memo skips re-rendering a component when its props are unchanged.
  • useMemo caches computed values; useCallback caches functions.
  • Use React.lazy for code splitting and stable keys for lists.

mcqs.q: What does React.memo do?
options: It skips re-rendering a component when its props have not changed
It makes the component load faster from the server
mcqs.why: React.memo compares the new props with the previous ones and reuses the last render when they are unchanged.

mcqs.q: What does useMemo cache?
options: A computed value, recomputed only when its dependencies change
mcqs.why: useMemo memoises the result of an expensive calculation and returns the cached value until a dependency changes.

mcqs.q: What does useCallback cache?
options: A function, so its identity stays stable across renders
mcqs.why: useCallback returns the same function reference until its dependencies change, which keeps memoised children from re-rendering.

mcqs.q: How does React.lazy help performance?
options: It loads a component's code only when that component is first needed
mcqs.why: React.lazy code-splits: the chunk for a heavy page is fetched only when the user opens it, so the first load stays small.

mcqs.q: Why do list items need a stable key prop?
options: Keys make the list look nicer
Keys tell React which item is which, so it updates only changed rows
mcqs.why: Stable keys let React match old and new items, so it reuses DOM nodes and only updates what actually changed.

tasks.title: Fill in the blank
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing hook so the sorted list is only recomputed when items changes.
tasks.code: const sorted = ___(() => items.sort((a, b) => a - b), [items]);
tasks.answer: useMemo caches the sorted result and recomputes it only when items changes.
tasks.hint: Which hook caches a computed value?
